name: Treaty with the Seneca, 1842 (Compromise Treaty of Buffalo Creek)
promises: The Seneca would keep the Cattaraugus and Allegany reservations with the same right and title they held before the 1838 sale, which this compact partly rescinded (indenture, Articles 1 and 7).

The Buffalo Creek and Tonawanda reservations went to Thomas Ludlow Ogden and Joseph Fellows for a price set by arbitrators, one named by the US Secretary of War, on the basis that the Indian title to all four reservations was worth $202,000 (Articles 2 to 4).
Payment for individual Seneca improvements was to be paid to the President of the United States and distributed to the owners under the War Department's direction (Article 5).
The parties would ask the United States to protect remaining Seneca lands in New York from all taxes and road or highway assessments (Article 9).

breaches.what: The Court of Claims held that the Trade and Intercourse Act of 1790 made the United States responsible for seeing that the Seneca received a conscionable price in the 1842 sale (and those of 1797 and 1826), reversing the Commission's 1963 dismissal.

breaches.quote: The Buffalo Creek and Tonawanda reservations were lost.

landTaken: 62,720 acres: the Tonawanda Reservation (12,800 acres) and the Buffalo Creek Reservation (49,920 acres) (Indian Claims Commission, 1972).
compensation: $133,768.96 was paid for the 1842 cession. The Commission's 1972 determination set $632,231.04 for it; the stipulated final award of November 22, 1972 in Dockets 342-A and 368-A was $5,466,615.04 for the 1797, 1826 and 1842 cessions together. The Tonawanda Band bought back 7,549 acres of its own reservation from the Ogden Land Company in 1857 for $153,742.55 (Commission, 1972).
today: Allegany and Cattaraugus, returned by this compact, remain Seneca Nation territories; the Tonawanda Band holds the part of its reservation it repurchased under the 1857 treaty.

nationVoice.summary: The Nation's archive describes the 1842 treaty as a compromise of a fraudulent 1838 treaty that restored Allegany and Cattaraugus but lost Buffalo Creek and Tonawanda.

openQuestions: Whether the United States acted on Article 9's request to protect Seneca lands from New York taxes, and the later tax disputes, were not researched.
The 1965 Court of Claims opinion was not opened directly and its exact date is not recorded.
How the ICC award was divided between the Seneca Nation and the Tonawanda Band was not found.

Audit 2026-11-08: all figures, articles and dates checked against the 1842 text, 28 Ind. Cl. Comm. 12 and the November 22, 1972 final award, and held. The 1972 award made the May 1972 adjudicated order final by stipulation; the unconscionability finding itself was adjudicated, so claims-commission stays.
